newsitem.title: CHINA: Extent of Thai central bank loans surprises HK.
newsitem.headline: Extent of Thai central bank loans surprises HK.

text.p: Thailand surprised Hong Kong fund managers and analysts by disclosing on Tuesday that its central bank had lent in excess of US$16 billion to debt-laden finance companies.
And eyebrows raised further when the central bank pledged to guarantee the debt repayments and deposits of 42 finance companies suspended on Tuesday for a crippling bad debt burden.
"I don't see how they can do that," said Ken Davies, senior regional economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit.
"Presumably the (International Monetary Fund) will put in some kind of ring-fence to try and ensure they stop short of giving a blank cheque..."
Few analysts in Hong Kong were prepared to speak openly about the economic survival package unveiled by Thailand on Tuesday.
One fund manager said his company was warned recently in a personal meeting with senior government officials "to stop trashing the baht" in its public comments in Hong Kong.

"That (US$16 billion) seems to be an awfully big number to have lent out," said one fund manager, who declined to be identified. "Most people were surprised by that. It's time to turn the lights out and go home."
Said another fund manager who also did not want to be identified: "That is a phenomenal amount of money. Everyone is surprised by that. That's a good portion of their foreign exchange position."

Sixteen finance companies had already been suspended and the additional 42 named on Tuesday means that only 33 of 91 finance companies will still be operating. Sources said smaller banks could fall prey to central bank action in the next few days.
A credit line from the International Monetary Fund (IMF), which has been holding discussions with Thailand for the past few weeks, is now considered virtually inevitable.
But the extent of the IMF's financial involvement remained unclear late on Tuesday.
"IMF involvement is useless if it hinges on these handouts," said Davies.

Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya said Thailand hoped to raise US$12-US$15 billion in loans from foreign countries and the IMF, and established a target of maintaining US$25 billion in foreign exchange reserves.

"At the end of the day, creditors, in particular foreign investors, will not return in sizeable force to the market unless they have confidence that good money will not be thrown after bad," the first fund manager said.
"Only then can we see a bottom on the baht and a peak in real interest rates, which are the necessary pre-conditions for a recovery in the financial markets."
The second fund manager said the medicine had been identified but they were less convinced that the prescription to recovery would be rigorously pursued.
"It's all very well saying this is what they're going to do, but when they actually do it and find there's an awful lot of pain attached it might be extremely difficult for these guys," he said.

"(Political upheaval) is the normal situation in Thailand and you can expect that it won't be any different this time. It would be nice but unrealistic to expect these guys to pull together and get this sorted out."
